items.text: **Anticholinergic medications** (antimuscarinics) are a cornerstone of urologic pharmacotherapy, primarily for **overactive bladder (OAB)** and **neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD)**.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[2]](#ref2)</sup> They block **muscarinic receptors (M2 and M3) in the detrusor muscle**, inhibiting involuntary contractions, increasing bladder capacity, and reducing urgency and frequency.

The class has six FDA-approved agents with broadly similar efficacy but meaningfully different tolerability, CNS penetration, and dementia-risk profiles. The **2022 SUFU White Paper** on anticholinergics and dementia risk and the **2024 AUA/SUFU OAB guideline** together have shifted contemporary practice toward β3-agonist-first positioning for many OAB patients, with anticholinergics reserved for specific indications, combination therapy, or patient-specific factors.
- **M3 receptors** produce **direct detrusor smooth muscle contraction** via extracellular calcium entry (L-type channels) + Rho kinase activation
- **M2 receptors** (more numerous) **facilitate M3-mediated contractions** and can reverse β-adrenoceptor-mediated relaxation<sup>[[3]](#ref3)[[4]](#ref4)</sup>
- **Antagonism of M3** → inhibition of detrusor contraction → increased bladder capacity + reduced urgency
- **Off-target effects** at other muscarinic receptor populations → the class side-effect profile
- **Minimal CNS penetration:** **trospium** (quaternary amine — poorly crosses BBB)<sup>[[3]](#ref3)[[6]](#ref6)</sup>
International agents not available in the US include **imidafenacin**, **propiverine**, and **propantheline**.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[3]](#ref3)</sup>
- Benefit over placebo is real but modest: about **0.85 fewer voids and 0.85 fewer urgency episodes per 24 hours** in the 2023 Cochrane review<sup>[[1]](#ref1)</sup>
- Placebo response is substantial (30–47% for incontinence) — a durable reminder that behavioral therapy and regression-to-mean matter
**Solifenacin vs. IR tolterodine** — solifenacin superior:
- Patient-reported cure/improvement (RR 1.25)
**Fesoterodine 8 mg vs. ER tolterodine** — fesoterodine superior for all efficacy endpoints, but **higher withdrawal** (RR 1.45) and **higher dry mouth** (RR 1.80)
**Tolterodine vs. oxybutynin** — similar efficacy; tolterodine has **less dry mouth** (RR 0.65) and **fewer withdrawals for adverse events** (RR 0.52)
**Extended-release > immediate-release** — similar efficacy, significantly less dry mouth in ER formulations
- **Tolterodine 1/2/4 mg:** similar efficacy; higher dose → more dry mouth
- **Solifenacin 5 vs. 10 mg:** 10 mg more effective but more dry mouth
**French case-control study (4,810 cases, 24,050 controls):** OAB anticholinergic use → OR 1.23 for dementia, with clear **dose-response relationship**:
- **Oxybutynin and solifenacin** — marked increased risk<sup>[[10]](#ref10)[[11]](#ref11)</sup>

- **Trospium** — limited brain penetration supports consideration when an antimuscarinic is needed; absence of an association in an individual study does not establish long-term cognitive safety.<sup>[[13]](#ref13)[[14]](#ref14)</sup>

**Pooled data:** a 2025 meta-analysis of eight observational studies found a **~20% higher dementia risk** with OAB anticholinergics versus no drug therapy (RR 1.2, 95% CI 1.09–1.32) and a higher risk than with mirabegron (RR 1.28); heterogeneity was very high, and confounding by indication remains possible.<sup>[[26]](#ref26)</sup>
- Lower CNS penetration with trospium, darifenacin and fesoterodine is a **theoretical advantage**, not proof of a safest agent<sup>[[14]](#ref14)</sup>

Anticholinergic blockade of acetylcholine in the brain disrupts cholinergic neurotransmission critical for learning and memory. Agents with greater CNS penetration (oxybutynin) pose higher cognitive risk than those with limited CNS penetration (trospium).<sup>[[3]](#ref3)[[12]](#ref12)</sup>

**However,** one propensity-matched cohort study (782 pairs, adults with normal cognition, MCI or dementia) found **no significant association** with clinically relevant cognitive decline, though dose and duration were unknown and oxybutynin/tolterodine users trended higher (CDR OR 1.65, 95% CI 0.98–2.77). The signal is not bulletproof, and residual confounding remains a concern.<sup>[[27]](#ref27)</sup>
- **Uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma** (the 2024 AUA/SUFU guideline advises extreme caution in any narrow-angle glaucoma and coordination with the treating ophthalmologist)<sup>[[14]](#ref14)</sup>
- **Urinary retention** (relative → absolute depending on severity)
- Use with **extreme caution** in narrow-angle glaucoma, impaired gastric emptying, or history of urinary retention
**2024 AUA/SUFU OAB guideline** positions pharmacotherapy as:<sup>[[14]](#ref14)</sup>
- Offer behavioral measures and discuss **β3-agonists or antimuscarinics** according to symptoms, adverse effects and preferences.

- **Botulinum toxin, sacral neuromodulation and PTNS** need not await completion of a fixed medication ladder; the guideline permits their selection without prior drug trials through shared decision-making.

**EAU 2026 (non-neurogenic female LUTS)** offers anticholinergics to women with OAB who fail conservative management (Strong) and advises shared decision-making, extended-release formulations whenever possible, early review of efficacy and adverse effects, and, if a drug fails, dose escalation, a different formulation or a β3 agonist alone or combined (all Strong). Immediate-release products allow flexible or on-demand dosing but cause more adverse events. EAU finds no anticholinergic clearly superior for cure or improvement and reports that most patients stop within three months. For older women it advises caution with long-term use, especially with existing or risk of cognitive dysfunction, and assessment of anticholinergic burden (Strong). Cognitive harm is cumulative with exposure (level 2); oxybutynin may worsen cognition, while darifenacin, fesoterodine, solifenacin and trospium have not been shown to in short-term studies (level 1b).<sup>[[31]](#ref31)</sup>
- **Combination therapy** — synergistic effect in patients with suboptimal monotherapy
- **Specific subpopulations** where antimuscarinic evidence is stronger (NLUTD, pediatric)
- **Elderly patient with cognitive concerns** — use β3-agonist or trospium
- **Active cognitive impairment / dementia** — avoid where an alternative exists
- **Severe BPH with high PVR** — worsens retention

Long-term adherence is **suboptimal** — pooled 1-year persistence is about 12-25% for antimuscarinics versus 32-38% for mirabegron.<sup>[[14]](#ref14)</sup> Drivers of discontinuation: dry mouth, constipation, cognitive side effects, inadequate efficacy.

**Antimuscarinic + β3-agonist** (e.g., **solifenacin 5 mg + mirabegron 25–50 mg**) provides **superior efficacy** vs. monotherapy in patients with partial response — SYNERGY and SYNERGY II showed this against each drug alone; in BESIDE, the combination beat solifenacin 5 mg but not 10 mg.<sup>[[15]](#ref15)[[16]](#ref16)</sup> The AUA/SUFU 2024 guideline offers different-class combination after inadequate single-drug response (Conditional Recommendation, Grade B); in SYNERGY II, adverse events were 49% with combination versus 41-44% with monotherapy.<sup>[[14]](#ref14)</sup>
- **Additional urgency/incontinence reduction**
- **Increased anticholinergic side effects** vs. β3-agonist alone — so the choice is a trade-off
Antimuscarinics are **first-line pharmacotherapy** for bladder storage dysfunction in NLUTD:<sup>[[17]](#ref17)[[18]](#ref18)[[19]](#ref19)</sup>
- **Intravesical oxybutynin** — delivers the drug locally with reduced systemic absorption; a valuable option in CIC-dependent NLUTD patients with systemic intolerance

**Oxybutynin** is the most-used agent — effective at increasing capacity, lowering storage pressures, abolishing overactive contractions. Mirabegron and (rarely) gabapentin are alternatives in intolerant patients.<sup>[[20]](#ref20)</sup>

Antimuscarinics benefit men with **predominantly storage symptoms** and coexisting BPH, alone or combined with an α-blocker; the AUA/SUFU 2024 guideline supports antimuscarinic or β3 monotherapy, or α-blocker plus either class (Conditional Recommendation, Grade B). Antimuscarinics may raise PVR slightly but have not been associated with significantly more retention in men with BPH-related obstruction, although effects with a PVR above 200 mL are not well studied. Combination with an α-blocker improves OAB symptoms more than α-blocker alone. **Check PVR before initiation and at follow-up.** The AUA BPH guideline (2026) likewise allows an antimuscarinic alone or with an α-blocker for moderate-to-severe predominant storage LUTS (Conditional Recommendation, Grade C), and adds behavioral measures when storage symptoms persist on medication.<sup>[[14]](#ref14)[[21]](#ref21)[[22]](#ref22)[[30]](#ref30)</sup>

With inadequate response, intolerance or preference for a procedure, discuss **minimally invasive therapies**. Prior medication failure is not a universal prerequisite:<sup>[[14]](#ref14)[[23]](#ref23)</sup>
- **Intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA** (100 U for idiopathic OAB; 200 U for NLUTD)
- **Posterior tibial nerve stimulation** (PTNS, eCoin, Revi)
- [β3-adrenergic agonists](/docs/foundations/pharmacology/storage-oab/beta3-agonists) — companion pharmacologic class
- [Desmopressin](/docs/foundations/pharmacology/storage-oab/desmopressin) — for nocturnal polyuria
